To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the clustering evolution of galaxies with different spectral type is consistent with the linear growth of mass clustering, with the clustering amplitude of star-forming galaxies increasing with redshift, while the clustering amplitude of passive galaxies decreases.
the clustering of star-forming galaxies evolves with cosmic time in a way that is consistent with the growth of the underlying mass fluctuations.
the evolution of the clustering of star-forming galaxies with spectral types can be explained by the growth of the linear clustering of massive dark matter haloes.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the evolution of galaxy clustering as a function of galaxy type, from the present epoch to z~1, and with the interpretation of these results in terms of the assembly of galaxies in the hierarchical clustering scenario.
the evolution of the spatial distribution of galaxies in the nearby universe.
the evolution of the spatial distribution of galaxies in the Universe.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the observed evolution of clustering is a consequence of a combination of the growth of mass fluctuations and of the progressive assembly of massive galaxies in the densest regions, with a strong dependence on spectral types.

the clustering evolution of galaxies with different spectral properties is in line with a scenario in which massive ellipticals are already in place in the densest regions of the Universe, whereas the star formation activity is more intense in the higher-density environments.

the observed evolution of galaxy clustering with spectral type is consistent with a hierarchical scenario where the assembly of galaxies is driven by a progressive increase in the density of the environment in which star formation takes place.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

(1) the clustering of galaxies is evolving differently depending on spectral type; (2) the evolution of the clustering of early-type galaxies is similar to that of the mass fluctuations, indicating that these galaxies have already assembled most of their mass at z~1.3; (3) the clustering of late-type galaxies is evolving faster than the mass fluctuations, suggesting that star formation is progressively increasing, back in time, going from low-density to high-density regions of the Universe.
, at least for massive galaxies, the observed clustering evolution is in good agreement with the hierarchical growth of dark matter halos.

the evolution of clustering is a powerful tool to study galaxy evolution, and that the evolution of the clustering of galaxies with different spectral type provides important information on the assembly history of galaxies.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the clustering properties of the two main galaxy populations (star-forming vs. early-type galaxies) are different and evolving with time in a way that is not easily reconciled within the standard LCDM model.
the evolution of galaxy clustering is a powerful probe of galaxy evolution, as it can constrain the evolution of galaxy properties with time and their dependence with environment.
galaxy evolution is a complex phenomenon and that the study of galaxy clustering can be an important tool to understand the processes that are responsible for galaxy formation.
